photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard; photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: The postcard shows a named Mohawk chief in full regalia (feather headdress, beaded bandolier bag, tunic, fringed leggings) photographed at Kahnawake, a Mohawk community, so it documents Mohawk dress and craft.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard; photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: The photograph shows a group of Mohawk men, women, and children in regalia (headdresses, fringed garments, beadwork) posing in front of a building at Kahnawake (Caughnawaga), a documented Mohawk community — a clear documentary photo of the people in traditional dress.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard; photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: The photograph documents a Mohawk (Kahnawake) family in regalia at a public event in 1939, a genuine documentary photo of the people's dress and communal life.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard (black & white with colour); photographic print
photo.reason: The postcard shows a Mohawk (Iroquois) man from Caughnawaga (Kahnawake), Quebec, posed in regalia with a bow and arrow, documenting Mohawk dress and material culture.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard; photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: Studio postcard portrait of Go-Won-Go Mohawk, a Native American (Mohawk-identified) performer, shown wearing a beaded headband, feathered ornament, and beaded/quilled jacket typical of Wild West-show "Indian" stage costume; this is a documentary photograph of a Mohawk person in decorated dress, fitting the claimed ethnicity.

household.name: Cradleboard
household.title: Cradleboard
household.reason: The image shows a painted wooden cradleboard with floral rosette designs typical of Mohawk/Haudenosaunee craft, consistent with the claimed ethnicity and category.

household.name: basket
household.title: basket
household.reason: A "fancy basket" made from black ash splints and sweetgrass with curled decorative elements is a well-documented Haudenosaunee/Mohawk (Akwesasne) craft tradition, and the museum explicitly attributes it to Mohawk (Akwesasne) makers.
